title: Sudama
body:
Sudama

Krishna and Sudama shared a deep bond of friendship from their days as students under Guru Sandipani, learning together the sacred scriptures and the ways of dharma. Though Krishna was of royal lineage and Sudama came from a humble brahmana family, their friendship was pure and unwavering. One day their guru sent the two into the forest to gather firewood, and the food for their journey was entrusted to Sudama. As they worked, a torrential rain broke out, and the two friends climbed separate trees to escape it. Growing unbearably hungry and forgetting Krishna for a moment, Sudama ate all the food himself. When the rain passed and Krishna asked whether any food remained, Sudama admitted what he had done; Krishna only smiled and said it was fine. The memory of that kindness stayed in Sudama's heart ever after.
Years passed, and both friends completed their education. Krishna became the ruler of Mathura and later Dwaraka, while Sudama, devoted to his duties as a brahmana, lived in great simplicity and poverty. He married a noble-hearted woman named Susheela, and together they had twenty-seven children; despite his learning and righteousness, he could scarcely provide even the barest necessities for his family, yet he never once complained. At last Susheela, seeing their children suffer from hunger, urged him to seek help from his old friend Krishna, certain that the protector of all would not turn him away. Reluctant, and unwilling to visit a king empty-handed, Sudama agreed only when Susheela borrowed a handful of beaten rice from a neighbor and tied it in a small cloth as an offering.
The journey to Dwaraka was long and hard, and Sudama's feet bled upon the harsh terrain, but his heart was full of hope at the thought of seeing his friend after so many years. Yet at the palace gates the guards, seeing his tattered clothes and frail body, mocked him, saying the king had no time for beggars. Heartbroken, Sudama turned to leave — but word of his arrival reached Krishna, who rushed to the gates and, seeing his long-lost friend, embraced him with tears of joy. Krishna personally escorted him into the palace, seated him upon His own throne, and, to the astonishment of the queens and courtiers, washed Sudama's wounded feet with His own hands, anointing them with sandalwood paste and fragrant oils. Rukmini herself, the Goddess Lakshmi, served him food, as Krishna comforted his friend and reminisced with him about their days in the gurukula.
As they spoke, Krishna noticed a small cloth tied at Sudama's waist. Reaching for it playfully, He discovered the handful of beaten rice, and delighting in the humble gift, He placed a morsel in His mouth and relished it. As He reached for a second, Devi Rukmini gently stopped Him, saying that a single bite was enough to grant Sudama all the wealth he could ever need. Sudama, unaware of the divine exchange, spent the night in the palace and left the next morning without asking Krishna for anything, for the joy of seeing his friend was more than enough. As he neared his home he was astounded to find a grand palace where his humble hut had stood, his wife and children in fine clothes, his household adorned with treasures. He understood then that Krishna had bestowed upon him immense prosperity without his ever having asked, and though wealthy now, he remained ever humble and devoted, knowing that true wealth lay not in riches but in the grace of the Lord.
